section.heading: 6.5 Least-Squares Problems
section.paragraph: Inconsistent systems arise often in applications. When a solution is demanded and none exists, the best one can do is to find an $$\textbf{x}$$ that makes $$A\textbf{x}$$ as close as possible to $$\textbf{b}$$ .

Think of $$A\textbf{x}$$ as an approximation to $$\textbf{b}$$ . The smaller the distance between $$\textbf{b}$$ and $$A\textbf{x}$$ , given by $$\parallel \textbf{b} - A\textbf{x} \parallel$$ , the better the approximation. The general least-squares problem is to find an $$\textbf{x}$$ that makes $$\parallel \textbf{b} - A\textbf{x} \parallel$$ as small as possible. The adjective “least-squares” arises from the fact that $$\parallel \textbf{b} - A\textbf{x} \parallel$$ is the square root of a sum of squares.

section.paragraph: The most important aspect of the least-squares problem is that no matter what $$\textbf{x}$$ we select, the vector $$A\textbf{x}$$ will necessarily be in the column space, $$\text{Col} A$$ . So we seek an $$\textbf{x}$$ that makes $$A\textbf{x}$$ the closest point in $$\text{Col} A$$ to $$\textbf{b}$$ . See Figure 1. (Of course, if $$\textbf{b}$$ happens to be in $$\text{Col} A$$ , then $$\textbf{b}$$ is $$A\textbf{x}$$ for some $$\textbf{x}$$ , and such an $$\textbf{x}$$ is a “least-squares solution.”)

section.heading: Solution of the General Least-Squares Problem
section.paragraph: Given $$A$$ and $$\textbf{b}$$ as above, apply the Best Approximation Theorem in Section 6.3 to the subspace $$\text{Col} A$$ . Let
$$\hat{\textbf{b}} = \text{proj} _{ \text{Col} A} \textbf{b}$$

Because $$\widehat{\textbf{b}}$$ is in the column space of $$A$$ , the equation $$A \textbf{x} = \hat{\textbf{b}}$$ is consistent, and there is an $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ such that
$$A \hat{\textbf{x}} = \hat{\textbf{b}}$$

Since $$\widehat{\textbf{b}}$$ is the closest point in $$\text{Col} A$$ to $$\textbf{b}$$ , a vector $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ is a least-squares solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ if and only if $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ satisfies (1). Such an $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a list of weights that will build $$\widehat{\textbf{b}}$$ out of the columns of $$A$$ . See Figure 2. [There are many solutions of (1) if the equation has free variables.]

section.paragraph: Suppose $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ satisfies $$A\widehat{\textbf{x}} = \widehat{\textbf{b}}$$ . By the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem in Section 6.3, the projection $$\widehat{\textbf{b}}$$ has the property that $$\textbf{b} - \widehat{\textbf{b}}$$ is orthogonal to $$\text{Col} \textit{A}$$ , so $$\textbf{b} - A\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ is orthogonal to each column of $$A$$ . If $$\textbf{a}_{j}$$ is any column of $$A$$ , then $$\textbf{a}_{j} \cdot (\textbf{b} - A\widehat{\textbf{x}}) = 0$$ , and $$\textbf{a}_{j}^{T}(\textbf{b} - A\widehat{\textbf{x}}) = 0$$ . Since each $$\textbf{a}_{j}^{T}$$ is a row of $$A^{T}$$ ,
$$A^{T} \left(\right. \textbf{b} - A \hat{\textbf{x}} \left.\right) = \textbf{0}$$
(This equation also follows from Theorem 3 in Section 6.1.) Thus
$$A^{T} \textbf{b} - A^{T} A \hat{\textbf{x}} & = & \textbf{0} A^{T} A \hat{\textbf{x}} & = & A^{T} \textbf{b}$$
These calculations show that each least-squares solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ satisfies the equation
$$\boxed{A^{T} A \textbf{x} = A^{T} \textbf{b}}$$
The matrix equation (3) represents a system of equations called the normal equations for $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ . A solution of (3) is often denoted by $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ .

note.title: Theorem ﻿13﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿13﻿
note.paragraph: The set of least-squares solutions of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ coincides with the nonempty set of solutions of the normal equations $$A^{T} A\textbf{x} = A^{T}{\textbf{b}}$$ .

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: As shown, the set of least-squares solutions is nonempty and each least-squares solution $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ satisfies the normal equations. Conversely, suppose $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ satisfies $$A^{T} A \hat{\textbf{x}}$$ $$= A^{T}{\textbf{b}}$$ . Then $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ satisfies (2), which shows that $$\textbf{b} - A\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ is orthogonal to the rows of $$A^{T}$$ and hence is orthogonal to the columns of $$A$$ . Since the columns of $$A$$ span $$\text{Col} A$$ , the vector $$\textbf{b} - A\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ is orthogonal to all of $$\text{Col} A$$ . Hence the equation
$$\textbf{b} = A \hat{\textbf{x}} + \left(\right. \textbf{b} - A \hat{\textbf{x}} \left.\right)$$

is a decomposition of $$\textbf{b}$$ into the sum of a vector in $$\text{Col} A$$ and a vector orthogonal to $$\text{Col} A$$ . By the uniqueness of the orthogonal decomposition, $$A\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ must be the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{b}$$ onto $$\text{Col} A$$ . That is, $$A\widehat{\textbf{x}} = \widehat{\textbf{b}}$$ , and $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ is a least-squares solution.

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Let $$\widehat{\textbf{x}} = R^{- 1}Q^{T}\mathbf{b}$$ . Then
$$A \hat{\textbf{x}} = Q R \hat{\textbf{x}} = Q R R^{- 1} Q^{T} \mathbf{b} = Q Q^{T} \mathbf{b}$$

By Theorem 12, the columns of $$Q$$ form an orthonormal basis for $$\text{Col} A$$ . Hence, by Theorem 10, $$QQ^{T}\mathbf{b}$$ is the orthogonal projection $$\widehat{\textbf{b}}$$ of $$\textbf{b}$$ onto $$\text{Col} A$$ . Then $$A\widehat{\textbf{x}} = \widehat{\textbf{b}}$$ , which shows that $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ is a least-squares solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ . The uniqueness of $$\widehat{\textbf{x}}$$ follows from Theorem 14.
